L342@P7: success, the things in it that were done well. Then I'm
L343@P7: going to show you a painting by Vermeer. By comparing

L345@P7: The key to the whole question of van Meegeren's
L346@P7: success is that he did not try to imitate the classical
L347@P7: Vermeer - the Vermeer we all think of, in the pictures
L348@P7: upstairs and in the Rijksmuseum and other great galleries. Van Meegeren chose Vermeer because he was a
L349@P7: Dutchman, because he was famous, and because his
L350@P7: works are very rare and very expensive. At the time van
L351@P7: Meegeren began, there were rumors all over Europe that
L352@P7: Andrew Mellon had offered more than one million
L353@P7: dollars-an enormous sum in those days, much greater
L354@P7: than it is today-for the famous Artist in His Studio,
L355@P7: now in the Vienna museum, which was then still in private hands. Van Meegeren, who had studied and knew
L356@P7: art history, took advantage of the fact that Vermeer's a
L357@P7: man we know little about. We have a group of works
L358@P7: done when Vermeer was mature, some of which are
L359@P7: dated. The work of his youth is missing. We have three
L360@P7: or four pictures that we believe were painted when he
L361@P7: was young. They are quite different; so different that
L362@P7: the one in Figure 2, Christ in the House of Mary and
L363@P7: Martha, in the Edinburgh museum, would not, I believe, have been attributed to him if it were not for
L364@P7: the fact that it bears his signature. (Even with the signature, it has taken people a long time to accept it as
L365@P7: his.) In other words, part of Vermeer's oeuvre is missing. Well, van Meegeren saw this gap and decided that
L366@P7: he would fill it. He wouldn't copy Vermeer: he would
L367@P7: create the missing part of Vermeer's oeuvre.

L420@P10: Now let's look at a painting that we are certain is by
L421@P10: Vermeer, and see if we can isolate the qualities that are
L422@P10: outstandingly his. The Girl Reading a Letter (Figure 8)
L423@P10: in the Rijksmuseum is recognized by everyone as Vermeer's work. It is a true expression of the spirit of seventeenth-century Holland: the feeling of peace, security,
L424@P10: and prosperity, the people's satisfaction with themselves,
L425@P10: the delight in material riches natural after a long period
L426@P10: of disaster and war, and the Protestant reserve and
L427@P10: reticence. These are all characteristic of Dutch painting
L428@P10: in the seventeenth century. The things that are personal to Vermeer are surely the picture's cool serenity,
L429@P10: the feeling of completely arrested movement and of
L430@P10: silence - the silence that Claudel describes so well in his
L431@P10: book L'Oeil Ecoute. There is also the fact that there is
L432@P10: nothing personal about the human being; the girl is
L433@P10: rather like the still life. She doesn't make you want to
L434@P10: put your arm around her waist. The delight you take
L435@P10: in the picture is entirely a visual, aesthetic delight, not
L436@P10: sensuous or emotional in any way.
L437@P10: Other important characteristics of Vermeer's style
L438@P10: are the incredibly lovely nuances of light and color that
L439@P10: run all through the picture, and the way each form is
L440@P10: surrounded by crystal clarity. Vermeer doesn't model
L441@P10: his form: he creates it by a series of colored facets, evoking rather than representing it. These are things that
L442@P10: occur in all pictures of Vermeer's mature period.
L443@P10: Compare this painting to Christ and the Pilgrims at
L444@P10: Emmaus. Once we've looked at a true Vermeer, the
L445@P10: faults of the other come out, the weaknesses, the failure
L446@P10: of the forger. None of the fundamental qualities of Vermeer's style, which reflect his special habits of feeling
L447@P10: and working, really exist in this other picture. The
L448@P10: clarity is gone: you don't feel the space around each
L449@P10: figure. There is a sentimentality to the head of Christ
L450@P10: that is quite foreign to anything of the real Vermeer.
L451@P10: It's actually much closer to our time. This is a major
L452@P10: weakness of any forger: he can't help interpreting past
L453@P10: art in terms of present predilections. The modeling is
L454@P10: not done in a series of facets, and the touch is greasy,
L455@P10: without that wonderful cool and measured quality that
L456@P10: you get in Vermeer. The overall harmony and balance
L457@P10: of Vermeer's pictures is also missing: look at van Meegeren's exaggerations, his insistence on the seams on the
L458@P10: sleeves and the highlights on the bread-impossible for
L459@P10: Vermeer.
L460@P10: In spite of these faults, van Meegeren was almost
L461@P10: successful. But he was almost successful not because of
L462@P10: the painting-I think that is plain, although stylistic
L463@P10-12: discussions cannot be fully convincing when they're 8. Girl Reading a Letter, by Vermeer. Riiksmuseum, Amsterdam. Photograph: Bruckmann based on illustrations rather than on actual works of
L464@P12: art -but because of the tricks he played. He was a remarkable confidence man, an extremely intelligent
L465@P12: crook. He created a provenance for the picture; he had
L466@P12: an intermediary who sold it for him; he got one of the
L467@P12: most prominent art historians-Abraham Bredius-to
L468@P12: write an article on it, which was published in The Burlington Magazine; it was then exhibited publicly. Finally
L469@P12: it was sold to the Boymans museum. The museum hesitated about taking it, although they were urged by
L470@P12: D. G. van Beuningen, an important collector who later
L471@P12: bought others of van Meegeren's works. In the end, the
L472@P12: museum was pushed into buying it because van Meegeren floated the rumor that the Rijksmuseum wanted
L473@P12: to get it.
L474@P12: At the end of the war I interrogated one of Goring's
L475@P12: agents, a man who represented him in Holland. It was
L476@P12: he who bought, or was the intermediary for Giring's
L477@P12: purchase of, a picture by van Meegeren after war was
L478@P12: declared. This man, Alois Miedel, told me the story of
L479@P12: how this happened, an instance of van Meegeren's astute
L480@P12: sense of timing and his exploitation of circumstance.
L481@P12: Miedel ran a small bank in Amsterdam. His wife was
L482@P12: Jewish, and they finally fled from Holland to Spain,
L483@P12: where I found and interrogated Miedel himself. He told
L484@P12: me he aided the Resistance under cover all through the
L485@P12: war, helping people to escape, out of loyalty to his Jewish wife. One night a man, who, he knew, was in the
L486@P12: Resistance, came to him and said, "Mr. Miedel, I know
L487@P12: you buy paintings for the Reichsmarschall and I have a
L488@P12: picture for you. But I will sell it to you only on one condition, and that is that you don't inquire where it came
L489@P12: from, because it belongs to an old Dutch family who
L490@P12: want to give the money to the Resistance." At that time
L491@P12: Miedel had staying with him an old friend, Heinrich
L492@P12: Hoffmann, Hitler's photographer and advisor on artistic
L493@P12: matters. Van Meegeren knew Hoffmann was there.
L494@P12: Miedel took the painting up to Hoffmann, who said,
L495@P12: "Why, it's a Vermeer! I want it for the Fiihrer." Miedel
L496@P12: went to the telephone and called Goring, who said he'd
L497@P12: send a plane for it the next day. Van Meegeren was a
L498@P12: real opportunist, and a very clever one.
L499@P12: He was finally arrested for financial collaboration,
L500@P12: since it was discovered that he had amassed an apparently
L501@P12: inexplicable fortune during the Occupation. Hoping to
L502@P12: get out of this collaboration charge, he admitted to
L503@P12: painting fake Vermeers. As a result he was sentenced to
L504@P12: only one year in jail. During his confession, and after
L505@P12: later studies, his tricks were revealed. He painted with
L506@P12: colors used in the seventeenth century, making only one
L507@P12: mistake, which came out in scientific analysis: he used
L508@P12: cobalt blue, not invented until the nineteenth century.
L509@P12: The medium he used was a substance similar to Bakelite.
L510@P12: When heated, this medium hardened, and the picture
L511@P12: seemed to have aged centuries in a few hours. As a consequence, the x-ray of a picture painted in this medium
L512@P12: looks like the x-ray of an old picture. It also resists solvents the way an old picture does. Van Meegeren's paintings were done on top of old ones that already had a
L513@P12: craquelure, and by heating and rolling them he transferred this craquelure to his own work.
L514@P12: What made it possible for him to get away with all
L515@P12: this was, of course, that soon after the first picture was
L516@P12: well publicized and bought by the Boymans museum,
L517@P12: war was declared. All paintings by Vermeer were hidden
L518@P12: away and the experts were in hiding, so it was impossible
L519@P12: to compare genuine Vermeers with van Meegeren's. Van
L520@P12: Meegeren's later pictures were much worse in quality.
L521@P12: I think there's no doubt that with time the forgeries
L522@P12: would have come out because of their stylistic weaknesses. That's a very important aspect of forgeries, particularly of old masters: a forger not only has to put himself into the skin of the artist and understand his times,
L523@P12: but he also has to realize what in the artist's work is
L524@P12: attractive to us today. Of course tastes change as time
L525@P12: passes. It's all very well to say that we can detect the forgeries easily now, stylistically, but every time I think of
L526@P12: it I feel, "There but for the grace of God go I." There's
L527@P12: no doubt that twenty years ago van Meegeren's paintings were much more appealing. Time is essential in a
L528@P12: case of this kind.
L529@P12: A curious consequence of today's sudden burst of
L530@P12: scientific knowledge is that we now tend to look too
L531@P12: closely at the physical components of a work of art. The
L532@P12: other day one of our most prominent scholars in Dutch
L533@P12: painting told me that when he saw the article in The
L534@P12: Burlington Magazine and the photographs of the Emmaus he said to his pupils, "That's a forgery." But then
L535@P12: he went to Holland, and when he saw the picture in front
L536@P12: of him, with its convincing craquelure, convincing colors,
L537@P12: convincing aging, he began to doubt his own first impression. There, close to it, he saw all the convincing details
L538@P12: and not what was wrong with the style.

L62: Some puzzles and their solutions can be seen as a microcosm of scientific progress, as readers build on each other’s comments and insights to discover something new, a process I experienced firsthand in many of my New York Times puzzle blogs. Puzzles can also deepen our understanding of scientific concepts, as in cite21†this puzzle†tierneylab.blogs.nytimes.com whose cite22†solution†tierneylab.blogs.nytimes.com provides insight into the second law of thermodynamics.
L63: And, as I argue in a recent cite23†Math Horizons article†dx.doi.org , I believe that our human love of solving puzzles is a reflection of the unique cognitive-emotional link that makes us the intelligent creatures we are. To coin a classically mixed neologism, we are Homo enigmatus — in more ways than one. Evolution has made us cognitive beings by giving us small internal rewards whenever we solve a puzzle — a very effective strategy.
L64: So, as we solve these monthly puzzles, we’ll try to look deeper into their analytic content and their emotional denouements, but we will also search for connections between our puzzles and problems in various fields of science. We’ll also explore some fascinating overarching themes that hold inexhaustible conceptual riches. Today’s puzzle highlights two such themes: randomness and information.

Then you can decide to either select the number you have seen or switch to the number you have not seen, held in the other hand, as your final choice.
L74: Is there a strategy that will give you a greater than 50 percent chance of choosing the larger number, no matter which two numbers I write down? (Update: The solution is now cite24†available here .)
L75: Since you know nothing whatsoever about the two numbers, the only thing you can do, it seems, is make random guesses. But can randomness generate information?
L76: Actually, randomness can be very powerful. When coupled with nonrandom selection and given enough time and iterations (such as in the process of evolution), randomness can exhaust almost all possible variations on a design, cite25†inevitably†wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com generating exquisite products that seem to have been planned with obsessive attention to detail.
L77: In some especially difficult problems, procedures called cite26†genetic algorithms†mathworld.wolfram.com , which simulate the interplay between randomness and selection characteristic of the evolutionary process, often provide better solutions than the best human experts. The crucial information that selection provides in this process is simple: It tells us which of two alternatives is better. Randomness, meanwhile, has the tedious job of working through a tremendous number of cases.
L78: So while randomness and selection are equal partners, the key information is provided by selection.
L79: With no way to know which alternative is better, what can random guesses achieve? Well, you could guess correctly and, improbably, hit a jackpot. This cite27†happens to all of us†wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com from time to time, convincing some people that they can access information in unexplained ways. But such luck tends to even out in the long run. After thousands of trials, the expected outcome of guessing in our game above is exactly 50 percent, no matter how many lucky guesses you have.
L80: This seems like a dead end.
L81: We know that randomness by itself is completely devoid of information. In Claude Shannon’s famous cite28†measure of the entropy of information†ieeexplore.ieee.org , a random guess is considered to have maximum disorder and consequently an information content of zero. We decry as pseudoscience any attempt to get meaningful information out of events that seem to be random, as in astrology, palmistry, synchronicity, cite29†apparent telepathy†wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com , or Tarot card reading.
